Slower Retail Sales Drag on Market
 
Plus, the SEC probes Nvidia and Disney is cutting costs
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
JOHN G MABANGLO/SHUTTERSTOCK
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

Tech stocks partially recovered toward the end of another tough session. With the Nasdaq Composite on track at one point during the day to lose 2%, the market clawed back losses later in the afternoon. Mid-session reports said that Anthropic planned to price its public offering above its initial range. The Nasdaq benchmark closed lower by 0.7%, and the S&P 500 index was off by 1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 1.6%, or 848 points.

 

Jensen Huang said he would go back to Nvidia if asked. During the day, before the company’s after-hours earnings report, Huang said in a statement that he “would be honored” to return as CEO if he was called to do so. The Journal reported near the end of the trading day that the Securities and Exchange Commission was investigating Nvidia. After the bell, Nvidia reported solid quarterly earnings. Shares fell 0.5% on the day.

 

Retail sales slowed in October. U.S. sales growth was just 0.2% in October month-over-month, after rising 0.8% in September. Treasury yields fell in the wake of the report, with the benchmark 10-year yield edging down to 5.105% from 5.122%. Some economists believe a boost from tax cuts is fading, with stock declines set to also weigh on spenders.

 

Home Depot slid as its chief executive stepped down. Ted Decker is stepping aside after a medical leave. The home-improvement retailer raised its full year forecast, with professional contractors a strong spot, even as homeowners are reluctant to take on larger projects. Its shares were off by 2.5%.

 

Disney is slashing costs. The company expects to hit $3 billion in annual savings by fiscal 2029, as new CEO Josh D’Amaro aims to transform the entertainment conglomerate for the streaming era. Shares were down 1.5%.

One Big Story

 
 
PAUL KIERNAN/WSJ
 

Large and creditworthy borrowers don’t normally keep real estate lenders awake at night. But a set of keys handed back by Brookfield is a wake-up call. Big investors are pragmatic about walking away from bad apartment deals.

 

Apartments were the hottest real estate trade of 2021 and 2022 when rents were booming and debt was cheap. But they have turned out to be a dud. High interest rates have wiped more than 20% off peak values and a construction boom tipped the apartment market into oversupply, destroying rent growth.
